awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of an On-board Localization and Navigation System for Autonomous Vehicles
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of a positioning system that provides reliable vehicle localization without relying on satellite-based or network-based positioning. The system addresses the challenge of guiding vehicles safely in regions where conventional positioning signals are weak, unavailable, or vulnerable to cyber-attacks. All current methods of vehicle localization depend on satellite signals prone to signal disruption and 3D mapping that is costly to produce and maintain, limiting their coverage to select areas. This new method ensures positioning using vehicle's on-board sensors and two-dimensional, widely available maps while a global positioning system (GPS) signal is not available or intentionally blocked by a cyberattack. This resilient approach enhances public safety, supports mobility across urban and rural areas, and bolsters economic productivity by enabling broader adoption of advanced transportation technologies.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This technology is based on the development of a sensor-driven localization framework that integrates vehicle kinematic dead reckoning with widely accessible, two-dimensional map information. The framework employs a kinematic dead reckoning methodology to estimate vehicle position from on-board vehicle sensors such as velocity, steering rate, steering angle, and yaw rate. To address the inherent drift associated with dead reckoning, an arc-length-based map-matching algorithm synchronizes the predicted trajectory with spatial features derived from map data. By merging temporal kinematic predictions with spatial map details, the system maintains high accuracy in environments where satellite-based positioning is unreliable or compromised. This technical innovation significantly advances positioning by offering a robust and reliable solution under challenging conditions.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Modern vehicles, including autonomous cars, delivery fleets, and advanced driver assistance systems, rely heavily on GPS for positioning and navigation. Yet GPS signals are frequently unavailable or unreliable in urban canyons, tunnels, parking structures, and areas affected by signal interference. This fundamental vulnerability represents a critical gap in the safety and reliability of next-generation transportation systems.

This NSF I-Corps project investigated the commercial potential of an on-board vehicle localization technology designed to provide accurate, lane-level positioning without dependence on GPS infrastructure. The technology uses onboard vehicle sensors — including wheel speed, steering angle, and inertial measurements — combined with lightweight map representations to determine vehicle position continuously, even when GPS is entirely unavailable. Unlike existing approaches that rely on expensive LiDAR sensors or high-definition mapping infrastructure, this system is designed to be low-cost, scalable, and deployable on standard vehicle hardware.

Through the NSF I-Corps program, the project team conducted extensive customer discovery activities over the award period. The team engaged with stakeholders across the automotive, autonomous systems, transportation, logistics, and public-sector communities to understand real-world localization challenges, customer requirements, and market opportunities. These conversations included discussions with automotive OEM engineers, fleet operators, transportation infrastructure organizations, autonomous vehicle developers, and technology integrators.

Customer discovery confirmed that GPS-denied localization is a widely recognized and unresolved challenge across multiple industries. Stakeholders consistently described operational disruptions, safety concerns, and reduced system reliability resulting from GPS outages and positioning uncertainty. The team found that current solutions — including high-cost sensor arrays and reliance on external positioning infrastructure — fail to meet the practical needs of many potential customers in terms of cost, scalability, and deployment simplicity.

The customer discovery process helped the team refine its understanding of target markets and identify the customer segments with the greatest near-term need for resilient localization capabilities. Key insights included the importance of system integration with existing vehicle architectures, the value of real-time positioning confidence estimation for safe decision-making, and the need for solutions that do not require expensive mapping campaigns or specialized hardware.

The project produced several important outcomes. The team validated strong market demand for GPS-independent localization across transportation and mobility sectors. A refined value proposition was developed based directly on stakeholder feedback, aligning the technology's capabilities with documented customer needs. The team identified promising commercialization pathways including direct technology licensing, OEM partnerships, and startup formation. Following the award period, commercialization activities have advanced to include a PCT international patent filing and active engagement with automotive OEM partners, reflecting the market readiness built through the I-Corps process, participate NSF Accelcorp, won grants to extend the development.

Participation in the NSF I-Corps program provided the team with significant entrepreneurial training and professional development. Team members gained practical experience in customer discovery methodology, business model development, market analysis, and technology commercialization strategy. These skills have strengthened the team's ability to translate a research innovation into a product capable of generating real-world impact.

The broader societal significance of this work lies in its potential to improve the safety, reliability, and accessibility of autonomous and connected vehicle technologies. By enabling vehicles to maintain accurate positioning without GPS, this technology supports safer transportation systems, more resilient mobility infrastructure, and greater public confidence in emerging autonomous technologies.
